statement: Two players take turns removing coins from a single pile. On each turn a player must remove a positive perfect square number of coins ($1$, $4$, $9$, $16$, and so on), never more than the pile holds. The player who removes the last coin wins. For how many starting pile sizes $n$ with $1 \le n \le 40$ can the second player guarantee a win?

hints: Work out who wins for piles of $1, 2, 3, \ldots$ coins, one size at a time.

A size is losing for the player about to move if every move leads to a winning size, and winning if some move leads to a losing size. The early losing sizes look periodic, but a new move appears at every perfect square, so check the pattern instead of trusting it.
The losing sizes up to $22$ are $2, 5, 7, 10, 12, 15, 17, 20, 22$. Then $25$ is winning, since the player to move takes everything, so the table has to be continued size by size up to $40$.

solutions.reliable: Call a size losing if the player about to move loses with best play; $0$ is losing. While only the moves $1, 4, 9, 16$ exist, the losing sizes are those leaving remainder $0$ or $2$ when divided by $5$: these moves change the remainder by $1$ or $4$, so from remainder $0$ they reach $4$ or $1$ and from remainder $2$ they reach $1$ or $3$, while from remainders $1, 3, 4$ the moves $1, 1, 4$ reach remainder $0$ or $2$. That gives the losing sizes $2, 5, 7, 10, 12, 15, 17, 20, 22$. At $25$ the move of $25$ coins appears and $25$ is winning, so the pattern must be checked from there. Sizes $23$ to $40$ other than $34$ and $39$ each have a move to a losing size: $23 \to 22$, $24 \to 20$, $25 \to 0$, $26 \to 22$, $27 \to 2$, $28 \to 12$, $29 \to 20$, $30 \to 5$, $31 \to 22$, $32 \to 7$, $33 \to 17$, $35 \to 34$, $36 \to 0$, $37 \to 12$, $38 \to 34$, $40 \to 39$. From $34$ the moves reach only $33, 30, 25, 18, 9$, and from $39$ only $38, 35, 30, 23, 14, 3$, all winning, so $34$ and $39$ are losing. The second player wins exactly at the $9 + 2 = 11$ losing sizes. The transferable idea: in a take-away game, work backwards one size at a time, and treat a pattern in small cases as a guess until you have shown that every move keeps it.
